A drone $D$ takes off from a point $P$ and flies at a constant angle of ${45}^{∘}$ to the horizontal. How fast is the drone gaining altitude if its speed is $42\,\text{km/h}?$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/40e0ae889d241c45464492ba3842d586effe528ab93b3554f6dbfb01d215c308.png)

Let $y$ be the drone's altitude and $z$ be the actual distance between the drone and its take-off point, as shown below.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ={45}^{∘},$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({45}^{∘}) & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{y}{z} \\ y & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}z) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=42\,\text{km/h}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 42=21\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the altitude is increasing at a rate of $21\sqrt{2}\,\text{km/h}.$
